idiom_name: one rule object per specification + And/Or/Not combinators (or plain predicates) + an optional translation visitor
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give every rule a single evaluation operation over a narrow candidate type (isSatisfiedBy(candidate)), let parameterized rules take their varying values as constructor parameters, and provide And/Or/Not combinators that hold children and return new specifications rather than mutating them (the composite form). Define an always-true and an always-false specification as identity elements so callers can start from a neutral rule. Apply specifications through a client - validator, selector, repository - and, if the same rule must also run in a store, add a translator/visitor that walks the rule tree and emits the store's query representation while keeping that translator out of the rule objects. In languages with algebraic data types or tagged unions, encode the combinators structurally rather than with inheritance. In class-based languages, prefer composition over inheritance for combinators. Always keep the candidate type as narrow as possible - an interface or an immutable view - to make leaf specs testable without constructing full aggregates.
code_sketch:
spec      = leaf(name, parameters)            # isSatisfiedBy(candidate) -> bool
composite = and(overdue(30), not(in_collection))  # combinators return new specs

candidates.filter(spec.isSatisfiedBy)             # in-memory validation
rows = repository.find(composite)                 # translated to a store query
pitfalls: Rules that read mutable state or have side effects destroy the pattern's testability and composability; evaluation must be a function of the candidate only.
Evaluating in memory and in a query from two independent definitions lets the rule drift; when a translator exists, test both paths against the same boundary candidates.
Combinators that mutate children, or specification instances shared across callers, leak state between rules that were meant to be independent.

Lambda capture in EF Core expression-based specifications: a closure capturing a mutable variable can silently produce different SQL on each call; always capture constructor-supplied values, not call-site temporaries.
Traversal-induced N+1: walking a lazy-loaded navigation property inside a leaf spec's translation triggers one query per candidate; resolve with eager loading in the adapter rather than at the leaf.

Putting business logic (logging, validation, non-deterministic calls) inside ToExpression — it is called multiple times during query construction, translation and compilation; side effects corrupt the evaluation contract.
Using Spec.False as the start of an AND-chain: False.And(anything) short-circuits to False, making subsequent combinators dead code; use Spec.True as the neutral AND identity instead.

Conflating a pure domain predicate (IsSatisfiedBy) with an expression-based query envelope (Expression<Func<T,bool>>) that also carries ordering, pagination or projection — Boolean algebra has no merge semantics for these fields.

Expression tree translation failures in EF Core: using untranslatable operations (Regex.Match, DateTime.ToString, complex string manipulation, custom C# methods) inside ToExpression causes runtime query generation failures; restrict leaf expressions to EF-Core-translatable operations.

Specification explosion: one class per trivial single-condition comparison bloats the codebase and makes the rule set harder to read than the original inline conditions; prefer a composable leaf library (equals, greaterThan, contains, inList) over a new type per field.
Forgetting identity elements: composing a dynamic OR chain without Spec.False as the base causes null checks and special-casing at every call site; define both neutral elements explicitly.

Treating a specification as a general-purpose interpreter: the Interpreter pattern applies the same AST to different evaluation contexts (pretty-print, optimize, translate); a specification's tree is evaluated in exactly one context (Boolean), so carrying a visitor interface on every leaf pollutes the domain with infrastructure concerns.

Wrong move: OR-ing a permission specification together with user-supplied filter specs at the same level -> a security predicate that is correct alone leaks rows once disjoined with a permissive filter (the LinqSpecs aggregation hole) -> combine security specs last, outside and above the discretionary filter tree, and test the combined query, not each spec in isolation.

Wrong move: relying on reference equality for structurally identical specifications -> caches keyed by spec instance miss and identical expression trees recompile per request (or worse, a shared mutable leaf poisons a cached compiled query) -> give specifications structural (value) equality, or cache compiled results keyed by the canonical structure.
